messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 77-year-old software engineer who has lived in the United States for over three decades, but the country he fled—a nation torn by civil war and ethnic cleansing—has never really released its grip on him. He arrived as a refugee in his mid-forties, alone at first, then sponsored by a church group that helped his wife join him two years later. They raised two children, now grown, and Kwame retired from a long career at a tech firm seven years ago. He still keeps a cluttered home office, monitors open-source projects, and writes small scripts to pass the time. But the work that once structured his days has become a cage of compulsive rumination, a way to keep his mind from wandering into places he cannot control.

The traumatic event that shattered his life occurred on a single afternoon in his home village. Soldiers under a regional strongman had been rounding up men for “interrogation.” Kwame, a university-educated engineer, was ordered at gunpoint to kneel in the dirt alongside dozens of others. He remembers not the sequence but the snapshots: the sun glinting off a bayonet, the grit of gravel on his palms, the stench of sweat and petrol from a burning vehicle nearby. A commander barked commands—words in a language Kwame understood only too well—and men were dragged away one by one. He heard gunfire and screaming, and then a sudden silence. For reasons he will never fully understand, he was shoved into a truck and left on a roadside miles away, told to run and never return. He did not know if his family had survived; he learned months later that many had not.

In the years after resettlement, Kwame threw himself into work, learning American coding standards, earning promotions, and building a stable life. But the snapshots never stopped. They come as sudden images: a man’s face contorted in terror, the cracked dashboard of the truck, the red dust rising behind the soldiers’ boots. Most of the time, Kwame can recall these moments with a strange emotional flatness—he describes it as watching a movie about someone else’s life, a stranger’s horror. Yet the pictures remain vivid, disjointed, each one a frozen frame that drops into his mind without warning. More disturbing is the sudden feeling of unreality that sometimes engulfs him. It can happen while he is standing in his kitchen, or reading a news article, or simply sitting in his armchair. A wave of detachment washes over him, as though he has stepped outside his own body, and the world around him becomes thin, distant, not quite real. These episodes terrify him more than the memories themselves, because they signal that he is losing his grip.

The triggers for these episodes are now woven into his daily life. The most potent is being given orders. When his wife asks him to take out the trash, or his doctor instructs him to schedule a test, or even when a customer-service voice on the phone says “please hold,” Kwame feels a surge of adrenaline and an almost physical recoil. He has come to believe that any command, however benign, carries a hidden threat—that compliance will lead to humiliation or harm. He avoids all situations where he might be told what to do. He no longer visits the hardware store because the clerk’s cheerful “what can I help you with?” feels like an interrogation. He stopped attending his church small group because the leader’s instructions to share felt like a demand.

His avoidance has grown wider. He has not gone grocery shopping in over a year; his wife brings home everything. He refuses invitations to family gatherings, community events, even walks in the neighborhood. People, he explains, are unpredictable. A stranger’s raised voice, a sudden gesture, a loud laugh—any of these could trigger a cascade of snapshots or that terrifying detaché feeling. The consequence is a profound isolation. His wife, whom he loves, has become his sole human contact, and she is exhausted. She has urged him for months to see a therapist; he agreed only after he found himself unable to leave the house to attend his granddaughter’s violin recital, frozen at the front door for twenty minutes, telling himself it was not safe.

To keep the memories and the numbing at bay, Kwame fills every waking moment with mental work. He solves algebraic puzzles in his head. He mentally rewrites old code, bug by bug. He memorizes baseball statistics from the 1950s—useless, intricate data that occupies the foreground of his mind. The moment his thoughts start to quiet, the images slip in, or the unreality begins. So he never stops. He has not had a full night’s sleep in years, because lying in the dark gives the snapshots room to play.

He came to my office for the first time last week, a tall, dignified man in a pressed shirt, who sat on the edge of the chair as if ready to flee. He told me, in a careful, measured voice, that he was afraid he was losing his sanity. He hoped I could give him something to make the feelings stop, but what he feared most was that if he began to talk about what happened, the numbness would crack, and he would drown in the emotions he had held at bay for decades. He wanted to be able to walk outside again, to see his granddaughter, to feel like the man his wife still believed he was. But he was not sure that man existed anymore.
